title: Counterarguments
description: Use concession and counterargument to structure, justify, and negotiate ideas related to counterarguments with appropriate B2 complexity.
objectives: Use concession and counterargument to structure, justify, and negotiate ideas related to counterarguments with appropriate B2 complexity.

stages.title: Understand meaning and form
stages.instructions: Read the concept, pattern, examples, contrast, common issue, and recap.

blocks.text: The communicative aim of this lesson is to use concession and counterargument to structure, justify, and negotiate ideas related to counterarguments with appropriate B2 complexity. The central language focus is concession and counterargument. In the context of society, media & debate, form and meaning work together: first identify the relationship between the ideas, then choose wording that makes that relationship clear to another person. At B2, organize the message so the listener can follow the claim, support, qualification, and practical consequence. Choose collocations and discourse markers that sound natural in professional and social contexts.

blocks.english: The speaker emphasized a fair point.
blocks.explanation: This model establishes the main communicative move.

blocks.english: Our response should account for concede that.
blocks.explanation: This model develops or qualifies the message.

blocks.text: Start with the model “The speaker emphasized a fair point.” It establishes a useful direction for the exchange. The second model, “Our response should account for concede that.” adds another layer: a reason, implication, contrast, or response. Notice how each complete chunk does a communicative job. Practice replacing one detail while preserving the original grammar, stance, and register. Then connect the revised sentence to a relevant consequence or example instead of changing topic abruptly.

A useful pattern for this lesson is: concession and counterargument. Use it when the situation genuinely calls for that meaning. Contrast matters: a direct factual statement presents information, while a qualified or hypothetical form changes the speaker's commitment to it. The choice should be driven by evidence, time reference, relationship, and purpose. In listening, pay attention not only to individual words but also to linkers, stress, and the speaker's degree of certainty.

blocks.title: Contrast
blocks.text: Compare a direct statement with language shaped by concession and counterargument; the intended meaning determines the form.

A common issue is to select an advanced-looking form without maintaining its meaning across the sentence. That can create a mismatch in time, stance, or register. Check three things: what happened or is being proposed, how certain the speaker is, and what response is expected. For counterarguments, clarity comes from a coherent message rather than maximum complexity. The later stages recycle the same vocabulary and expressions so that recognition becomes controlled production and then flexible interaction.

blocks.title: Common issue
blocks.text: Do not add complexity that changes the time reference, degree of certainty, or relationship with the listener.

stages.title: Listen for meaning and stance
stages.instructions: Listen first, then reveal the text and notice connections, register, and emphasis.

segments.text: To begin with, The speaker emphasized a fair point. Our response should account for concede that.
In this situation, Our response should account for concede that. This example illustrates counterargument clearly.
From another perspective, This example illustrates counterargument clearly. We should consider nevertheless carefully.
More specifically, We should consider nevertheless carefully. The discussion highlighted media coverage.
Even so, The discussion highlighted media coverage. A clear explanation addresses public perception directly.
As a result, A clear explanation addresses public perception directly. The speaker emphasized bias.
